newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - S.Africa CPI seen at 20-month high in Feb.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - S.Africa CPI seen at 20-month high in Feb.

text.p: South Africa's annual rate of consumer price inflation will have increased again in February to the highest level since June 1995, according to the consensus of 11 economists polled on Thursday.

However, the expected rise to 9.75 percent from 9.4 percent in January mainly reflects a low year-ago base. The month-on-month rate of increase is expected to slow to 0.45 percent after 1.3 percent in January.
The CPI data, due for release on March 27, will be the main focus of attention for local markets in the coming week.

But traders will also be keeping a watchful eye on the possible release of February trade data over the next week or two, which is expected to show an improved trade balance after disappointing figures in January.
Economists said that food prices were expected to have increased only modestly in February and they noted that February was generally a low survey month.

But inflation will have been stoked by substantial increases in telephone charges announced by state utility Telkom, as well as high new car prices which will increase the transport index despite a modest fall in fuel prices.

Consumer price inflation is likely to increase for a few more months as the final effects of the rand's sharp depreciation in 1996 feed through. But the CPI should peak at around 10 percent late in the first quarter or early in the second.
"We should see the top of the cycle at just above 10 percent in April," predicted Herman van Papendorp, economist at SMK Securities.
Pieter Calitz of life assurer Sanlam also saw a peak in April or May and said the rate should then come down to around 7.5 percent by year-end.
February trade data, due either next week or the week after according to officials, should show an improvement on January when a small surplus disappointed the market, analysts said.
"We continue to look for an improving trade balance and therefore for an improving current account in 1997," said Rand Merchant Bank Treasury economist Julia Roy.
The consensus was for a February trade surplus of 1.04 billion rand after 517.20 million rand in January.
For the full year, analysts expect strong exports -- helped by a lower rand -- and relatively weak imports to lead to a sharp improvement in the country's current acount position.
A Reuters survey released earlier on Thursday showed local and overseas economists expected the deficit to narrow to 3.65 billion rand in 1997 from 8.5 billion in 1996.
